classification_signals: The paper explicitly states its aim is 'to encourage psychiatrists to present the needs... to encourage architects to question psychiatrists...' (p. 23).
It outlines 'assumptions' and 'principles rather than with particulars' for design (p. 23).
It proposes 'Rules Deriving from the Patients' Needs' for architectural design (p. 24).

It synthesizes clinical observations and some cited research (e.g., Weckowicz's 'Notes on the Perceptual World of Schizophrenic Patients') to build a prescriptive argument for design, rather than presenting new empirical data or a systematic review.
title: Function as the Basis of Psychiatric Ward Design

findings.antecedent: failure in communication between client (psychiatrist) and architect
findings.consequent: monstrous and unsatisfactory mental hospitals, grave clinical and administrative difficulties
findings.quote: Hundreds of monstrous and unsatisfactory mental hospitals... are an eloquent testimony to the failure in communication

findings.antecedent: mentally ill people's needs (functional requirements)
findings.consequent: efficient building structure
findings.quote: from this an architect should be able to devise an efficient structure.

findings.antecedent: surroundings (for mentally ill people)
findings.consequent: ability to make the most of assets and aggravate disabilities as little as possible
findings.quote: require surroundings which allow them to make the most of their assets and which aggravate their disabilities as little as possible.

findings.antecedent: rupture in interpersonal relationships (alienation, social isolation)
findings.consequent: mentally ill people's common quality
findings.quote: only one quality common to all of them without exception: a rupture in interpersonal relationships resulting in alienation

findings.antecedent: primary changes in perception, thinking, feeling, motility (in mentally ill)
findings.consequent: disturbance in interpersonal relationships
findings.quote: This disturbance in interpersonal relationships is usually produced by primary changes in perception, thinking, feeling (affectivity) and sometimes motility.

findings.antecedent: interpersonal difficulties
findings.consequent: difficulties in perception, thinking, etc.
findings.quote: These interpersonal difficulties frequently aggravate the difficulties in perception, thinking, and so on.

findings.antecedent: psychiatric ward design
findings.consequent: influence vicious circle of interpersonal and perceptual difficulties for the better
findings.quote: The design of a psychiatric ward must incorporate ways of influencing this vicious circle for the better.

findings.antecedent: staff placement (in psychiatric ward design)
findings.consequent: provision of greatest amount of support, help and encouragement for patients
findings.quote: the staff must be placed so that they can provide the greatest amount of support, help and encouragement for the patients

findings.antecedent: opportunities for group activity (in psychiatric ward design)
findings.consequent: patients helping each other
findings.quote: The patients too must have every opportunity to help each other by means of group activity

findings.antecedent: changes in spatial perception (in schizophrenic people)
findings.consequent: uncertainty about the integrity of the self
findings.quote: changes in spatial perception are often accompanied by changes in perception of the body... huge corridors and unnecessarily enlarged spaces... are liable to enhance... uncertainty about the integrity of the self.

findings.antecedent: familiar surroundings seeming changed (due to visual perception changes)
findings.consequent: frightening uncertainty
findings.quote: Changes in visual perception so that familiar surroundings seem changed; the uncertainty which this generates may be frightening.

findings.antecedent: small, reassuring, easily encompassed spaces
findings.consequent: desirability for schizophrenic patients
findings.quote: Experimental evidence... suggests that small, reassuring, easily encompassed spaces are desirable.

findings.antecedent: small groups of 4-8 patients (who know each other well) living in comfortable surroundings, cared for by interpersonally skilled staff
findings.consequent: empathic support, lessened fear (for patients)
findings.quote: Such groups of four to eight people cared for by someone trained in interpersonal skills will give each other empathic support and lessen fear.

findings.antecedent: disturbing echoes and auditory peculiarities
findings.consequent: aggravation of auditory hallucinations (voices) in tense sick persons
findings.quote: Very often these [auditory hallucinations] appear mostly when the sick person is tense. Disturbing echoes and auditory peculiarities should be avoided in design.

findings.antecedent: ample provision of clocks, calendars, up-to-date newspapers, television, internal broadcast systems
findings.consequent: patients' attention focused on socially recognized 'real time'
findings.quote: The ample provision of clocks, calendars and up-to-date newspapers is necessary to remind patients that 'world time' is 'real time.' Television, properly used, and internal broadcast systems can all help to focus the patients' attention on the socially recognized time.

findings.antecedent: coarseness of institutional clothing, lack of pleasantly-textured fabrics and surfaces
findings.consequent: harm to mentally ill
findings.quote: The coarseness of institutional clothing and the lack of pleasantly-textured fabrics and surfaces in the surroundings have undoubtedly been harmful to the mentally ill.

findings.antecedent: properly functioning, well-ventilated spaces, sufficient number of toilets
findings.consequent: mitigation of hypersensitivity and changes in olfactory sense
findings.quote: Hypersensitivity and changes in this sense make properly functioning, well-ventilated and a sufficient number of toilets of even greater importance than in general hospitals.

findings.antecedent: good and congenial surroundings
findings.consequent: reduction of preoccupation with changes in body perception (hypochondriacal delusions)
findings.quote: It is probable that good and congenial surroundings can reduce preoccupation with these changes.

findings.antecedent: perceptual apparatus confusion (experiments)
findings.consequent: avoidance of such confusion in psychiatric wards
findings.quote: Experiments in perception show that our perceptual apparatus can easily be confused; such confusion must be avoided in psychiatric wards.

findings.antecedent: small group of people who know and understand each other
findings.consequent: stabilization of mood changes
findings.quote: A small group of people who know and understand each other tend to stabilize mood changes.

findings.antecedent: privacy and a place of one's own (for mentally ill)
findings.consequent: avoidance of being overwhelmed emotionally by suffering of companions
findings.quote: For them, privacy and a place of their own is essential if they are to avoid being overwhelmed emotionally by the suffering of their companions.

findings.antecedent: ward design (for patients with severe thinking difficulties)
findings.consequent: ease of biological life (washing, toilets, clothing/possessions storage)
findings.quote: The ward must therefore make the patients' biological life easy to live. Washing arrangements and toilets must be close at hand and easily located. Clothing and personal possessions too must be stored so that they can be kept nearby and be under the patients' own control

findings.antecedent: clearly labeled rooms (suitable size and color), patient's name on doors/lockers, mirrors in bedrooms/bathrooms (under patient control)
findings.consequent: help for patients with memory failure or impaired self-notion
findings.quote: rooms must be clearly labeled in letters of a suitable size and color... patient's name being clearly written on the doors of rooms and lockers can help here. Mirrors in bedrooms and bathrooms can help to remind one who one is.

findings.antecedent: overcrowding (too many people in a space for a lesser number)
findings.consequent: patients forced to interact, tread upon each other's toes
findings.quote: Too many people must not be forced to live or sleep in a space intended for a lesser number. Overcrowding forces people... literally to tread upon each other's toes.

findings.antecedent: overcrowding (in animals)
findings.consequent: major changes in adrenal glands, death (if unable to escape)
findings.quote: in animals, overcrowding alone can cause major changes in the adrenal glands... Some animals, if forced to live in overcrowded conditions from which they cannot escape, will die.

findings.antecedent: overconcentration (too many people forced to interact, e.g., 100 patients in a dayroom)
findings.consequent: harm to mentally ill, loss of hope of recovery
findings.quote: Too many people must not be forced to interact together... A dayroom in which 100 patients have to congregate would be harmful... It can so damage the mentally ill that they lose all hope of recovery.

findings.antecedent: overcrowding and overconcentration (in mental hospitals)
findings.consequent: harm to patients, psychological withdrawal from reality
findings.quote: Each is harmful, overconcentration probably being worse. Architects and psychiatrists have a very high responsibility to design buildings which do not lend themselves to overcrowding and in which overconcentration cannot take place.

findings.antecedent: opportunity for physical retreat (when patients feel threatened)
findings.consequent: less harm to patient than psychological withdrawal or physical resistance
findings.quote: When patients feel threatened they must... have the opportunity to retreat physically rather than be forced to resist physically or... into psychological withdrawal from reality. Physical retreat can easily be reversed; it is less likely to harm the patient than psychological withdrawal

findings.antecedent: patients having a place of their own (under their own control)
findings.consequent: benefit for patients
findings.quote: It follows that patients require a place of their own, as far as possible under their own control.

findings.antecedent: presence or absence of nest/den (for wild animals in zoos)
findings.consequent: difference between survival or death
findings.quote: Hediger has shown that for many wild animals incarcerated in zoos, the presence or absence of this nest or den makes the difference between the survival or death of the creature.

findings.antecedent: small room (approx. 50 sq ft) for psychotic people
findings.consequent: preference over twice that space in a dormitory with many people
findings.quote: for psychotic people, a small room of perhaps only 50 square foot floor space is much to be preferred to twice that space in a dormitory with many people.

findings.antecedent: groups of four to eight people
findings.consequent: formation of beneficial, supportive, constructive relationships
findings.quote: There is evidence that groups of four to eight people are especially liable to form beneficial, supportive and constructive relationships

findings.antecedent: presence of a nurse trained in group activity
findings.consequent: enhancement of beneficial relationships in groups of 4-8 patients
findings.quote: these can be enhanced by the presence of a nurse trained in group activity.

findings.antecedent: rooms having two or three people together (for gravely psychotic people)
findings.consequent: objectionable and harmful relationships
findings.quote: For gravely psychotic people, rooms having two or three together are nearly always objectionable and can be very harmful.

findings.antecedent: dormitories for from four to eight people with bed alcoves (as substitute for single rooms)
findings.consequent: best substitute for single rooms
findings.quote: if for some reason single rooms cannot be provided, then dormitories for from four to eight people with bed alcoves are the best substitute.

findings.antecedent: two or three people sleeping in a single room (for psychotic people)
findings.consequent: muddling of social and sexual status
findings.quote: Psychotic people are very often muddled about their social and sexual status. It would seem unwise to muddle them even more.

findings.antecedent: illusory administrative conveniences (security, supervision) allowed to endanger psycho-social needs of patients
findings.consequent: necessity of 'security' type building, neglect of psycho-social needs
findings.quote: Illusory administrative conveniences such as security and supervision, must not be allowed to endanger the psycho-social needs of the patients. The 'security' type of building is often necessary because the design of psychiatric wards wholly neglects the psycho-social needs of patients.

findings.antecedent: building itself expresses patient/staff needs
findings.consequent: patients and staff feel more secure, less reliance on mechanical aids
findings.quote: When the building is itself an expression of those needs, both patients and staff will, I believe, feel so much more secure themselves that they will not have to rely as much on mechanical aids.

findings.antecedent: ambiguity (in environment)
findings.consequent: tension (in well people), difficulty to bear (in mentally sick people)
findings.quote: Well people respond to ambiguity with tension... Mentally sick people, especially schizophrenics and old folks, find ambiguity and the uncertainty which accompanies it hard to bear.

findings.antecedent: avoidable ambiguities in function and structure of hospitals
findings.consequent: addition to patients' wretched condition (puzzlement, danger, distress)
findings.quote: It is important not to add to this wretched condition by avoidable ambiguities in the function and structure of hospitals supposed to help the sick.

findings.antecedent: huge system of corridors (in mental hospitals)
findings.consequent: disturbing perspectives, great strain on perceptual apparatus of psychotic, patients crouching/moving slowly/lying on floor
findings.quote: The extraordinary perspectives of these elongated corridors are disturbing even to the well and place a great strain on the perceptual apparatus of the psychotic. Anyone watching mentally ill people in these corridors can see how strange they find them.

findings.antecedent: too few opportunities for choice (in mental hospitals)
findings.consequent: difficulties for patients
findings.quote: Dr. J. Cummings emphasized that patients in mental hospitals have far too few opportunities for choice

findings.antecedent: too many opportunities for choice (in mental hospitals)
findings.consequent: difficulties for patients
findings.quote: Dr. M. Rejskind suggested that they had too many [choices].

findings.antecedent: choosing between many alternatives (even pleasant ones)
findings.consequent: tension and irritation (in well people)
findings.quote: Choosing between many alternatives, even when these are pleasant, produces tension and even irritation in well people.

findings.antecedent: limited everyday choices (food, clothing, recreation) and forced choice of intimate companions (from a mob of strangers) in mental hospitals
findings.consequent: opposite conditions to normal living, harm to patients
findings.quote: people incarcerated in these places have their everyday choices... limited, whereas they have to choose intimate companions from a mob of equally sick strangers

findings.antecedent: patient's personal living space having distinctive design (furniture, possessions, rugs, pictures, decorations, lighting)
findings.consequent: patients impressing personalities on surroundings, encouragement of individuality
findings.quote: the patient's personal living space must have something distinctive about it and the design should lend itself to placing furniture, small personal possessions, rugs, pictures, wall decorations and lighting so that patients can impress their personalities on their surroundings and be encouraged to do so.

findings.antecedent: suitable arrangements for patients to have small animals as pets on and near their wards
findings.consequent: benefit for patients
findings.quote: thought should be given to see how suitable arrangements could be made for patients to have small animals as pets on and near their wards.

findings.antecedent: sex segregation (in mental hospitals)
findings.consequent: patients forced to live in homosexual communities, not suitable for them
findings.quote: the cure, rigid segregation, was as bad as the disease; for mentally ill people are often forced to live in homosexual communities which are not suitable for them.

findings.antecedent: surroundings where schizophrenics meet people of the other sex
findings.consequent: maintenance of social skills for regulating relationships
findings.quote: Schizophrenics, then, require surroundings where they meet people of the other sex, so that they can maintain those social skills which our culture and most others require for regulating relationships between the sexes.

findings.antecedent: sex segregation
findings.consequent: desocialization, carelessness in dress, uncouthness, lack of pride in appearance, increase in auto-erotic and homoerotic activities
findings.quote: The danger of sex segregation is that it encourages desocialization by allowing the development of carelessness in dress, uncouthness and lack of pride in one's appearance. In addition... it assures an increase in ipsophilic (auto-erotic) and isophilic (homoerotic) activities.

findings.antecedent: schizophrenics' percepts determined more by retinal images than normal people's
findings.consequent: disordered size constancy
findings.quote: in schizophrenics, size constancy becomes disordered. Their percepts are determined to a greater extent by the retinal images than are the percepts of normal people.

findings.antecedent: disturbance of size constancy
findings.consequent: disturbed perception of distances between objects
findings.quote: a disturbance of size constancy would lead to a disturbed perception of distances between the objects.

findings.antecedent: size perceived as smaller
findings.consequent: distance perceived as longer
findings.quote: when the size is perceived as smaller, the distance is perceived as longer.

findings.antecedent: schizophrenics
findings.consequent: tendency to under-estimate sizes of objects seen at a distance
findings.quote: Schizophrenics tend to under-estimate the sizes of objects seen at a distance.

findings.antecedent: psychotics (particularly schizophrenics)
findings.consequent: tendency to over-estimate distance
findings.quote: psychotics, particularly schizophrenics, tend to over-estimate the distance.

findings.antecedent: schizophrenics over-estimating distance
findings.consequent: larger 'subjective space' than normal people, strain on cybernetic mechanisms, feeling small/lost in vast space
findings.quote: Schizophrenics, therefore, who tend to over-estimate distance, have a larger 'subjective space' than do normal people. This may put a great strain on their cybernetic mechanisms. They may feel small-lost in the vast space.

findings.antecedent: loss of ability to construct 'subjective space'
findings.consequent: many ambiguities, loss of sense of space, loss of feeling of reality, distortion of bodily image (feeling small)
findings.quote: This loss of the ability to construct 'subjective space' creates many ambiguities. It may lead to loss of sense of space-a loss of feeling of reality and distortion of the bodily image, as, for instance, feeling small.

findings.antecedent: schizophrenics' subjective space approaching Euclidean space more than normals' subjective space
findings.consequent: schizophrenics living in a more 'real' physical world than normals, difficulty encompassing subjective space, range too wide for scanning mechanism
findings.quote: schizophrenics live in a more 'real' physical world than normals do. Their subjective space approaches more the Euclidian space than does the subjective space of the normal people... The schizophrenic finds it more difficult to encompass his subjective space; the range is too wide for his scanning mechanism to operate.

findings.antecedent: environment exerting little strain on cybernetic mechanisms
findings.consequent: suitable environment for schizophrenic patient
findings.quote: the suitable environment is the one which exerts as little strain on these mechanisms as possible.

findings.antecedent: unambiguous, clearly defined situation (environmental)
findings.consequent: suitable environment for schizophrenic patient
findings.quote: It should confront the schizophrenic patient with an unambiguous, clearly defined situation.

findings.antecedent: large spaces, large wards, long corridors with interminable vistas
findings.consequent: unsuitability for person who has lost ability to foreshorten subjective space
findings.quote: Obviously, large spaces, like large wards and long corridors with their interminable vistas, are not suitable for a person who has lost the ability to foreshorten his subjective space.

findings.antecedent: larger spaces being circular (like horizon)
findings.consequent: better adaptation of senses than rectangular spaces
findings.quote: The larger spaces should be circular, as we are all living in a circular world (the horizon is round) and our senses are more adapted to a circular space than to a rectangular one.

findings.antecedent: scanning of large surface perpendicular to line of gaze (requiring constant change of range)
findings.consequent: additional strain on cybernetic mechanisms (in schizophrenic patients)
findings.quote: Scanning of a large surface perpendicular to the line of gaze requires a constant change of range in the scanning mechanism. This puts an additional strain on the cybernetic mechanisms

findings.antecedent: simple, unambiguous, functional furniture and objects in surroundings
findings.consequent: creation of unambiguous, simple, clearly defined world, demanding small number of choices from schizophrenic patient
findings.quote: The objects of his surrounding, for instance, furniture, should be simple, unambiguous and functional in their design. This will create an unambiguous, simple, clearly defined world which will demand a very small number of choices from the schizophrenic patient.

limitations: The paper acknowledges that it deals with 'principles rather than with particulars' (p. 23).

It notes that 'experimental evidence (and we have not nearly enough of this at the moment) suggests...' regarding small spaces (p. 24), indicating a reliance on theoretical deduction and clinical observation rather than extensive empirical data for all claims.

The arguments are largely based on understanding the subjective experience of mental illness and extrapolating design implications, rather than reporting on controlled architectural interventions and their measured outcomes.
minimum_safe_summary: This conceptual paper by Humphry Osmond (1957) argues that psychiatric ward design should be based on the functional needs and disabilities of mentally ill patients, particularly schizophrenics. Key findings include that large, ambiguous spaces and overcrowding are detrimental, while small, reassuring, and clearly defined spaces, opportunities for privacy, and social interaction in small groups are beneficial. The paper also highlights the importance of sensory considerations (e.g., avoiding disturbing echoes, providing pleasant textures) and the need for design to support patients' impaired perception, thinking, and social relating. Limitations include the paper's focus on principles rather than specific empirical data, relying on clinical observation and theoretical deduction.
